opus-5.5.text:
Well, the way I think about it, the pre-trained language model is still doing what it has always done: it's a generator of plausible guesses. It's a very good approximate retrieval engine. Given a prompt, it can produce candidate continuations, and in O1's case candidate chains of reasoning steps, that look like the kind of thing a human might write when solving a problem. That part hasn't fundamentally changed. What I don't think the pre-trained model does by itself is guarantee that any of those guesses are actually correct.

So when people see O1's improved accuracy on planning or math benchmarks, my reading is that the pre-trained model supplies the raw material, the space of candidate moves, and something on top of it is doing the selection. From what OpenAI has said publicly, and from what you can infer, there's a reinforcement learning phase that was trained on problems where you could check the answer, synthetic data where you know what's correct. That post-training shapes which chains of thought the model tends to generate. Then at inference time it spends a lot more compute, generating longer traces and presumably doing some kind of internal search or self-evaluation before committing to an answer.

If you put it in the generate-and-test framing that I keep coming back to, the LLM is the generator, and the improvement comes from bringing in some form of testing or verification, either baked in during training through RL with verifiable rewards, or done at inference by sampling and filtering. It's a bit like AlphaGo: the policy network proposes plausible moves, but the strength comes from search and evaluation on top of it. Nobody says the policy network alone "understands" Go.

That's why I've been careful to call O1 something more like a large reasoning model rather than just a large language model. It's a different beast. The pre-trained LLM is a necessary component, because without a good generator your search space is hopeless, but it isn't the thing doing the reasoning in the sense we'd want for guarantees. And you see that in our evaluations: on PlanBench, O1 does much better than the earlier models on standard Blocksworld problems, but as you scale up problem size, or use obfuscated domains where you can't lean on surface familiarity, the accuracy drops considerably, and the costs go way up. It's still not giving you correctness guarantees.

So the honest answer is that the pre-trained model gives you the intuition, the System 1 guesses, and O1's gains come from the machinery that turns those guesses into something closer to deliberate search. That's actually a vindication of the idea that you need verifiers in the loop. The open question is how much of that verification you can internalize into the model versus keeping external, sound verifiers around, which is what we argue for with the LLM-Modulo framework, especially when you care about guarantees rather than just better average-case accuracy.

r001.rationale: The response discusses performance on familiar versus obfuscated domains, but does not state that accuracy is higher where pre-training data is more abundant.

r002.rationale: It describes the pre-trained model generating candidate reasoning chains, but does not hypothesize that a smaller language model generates pseudo-action tokens to steer it.

r003.rationale: It says reinforcement learning shapes generated chains and that a good generator is necessary, but does not conjecture that greater base-model capacity lets reinforcement learning raise accuracy further.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the way I think about it is that the pre-trained language model in O1 is essentially the generator, and the important thing to understand is that by itself, the autoregressive LLM is doing what I have been calling approximate retrieval. It is giving you a plausible-looking completion, not something that it has verified. So when people saw O1 doing much better on things like the math benchmarks and on planning problems, the question is: what changed? The base model did not suddenly become a reasoner.

What I think happened, and OpenAI has been fairly cagey about the details, so some of this is my reconstruction, is that they used the pre-trained model as a very good proposal distribution. The model generates candidate chains of thought, intermediate steps, and then there is a reinforcement learning phase, and at inference time there is a search or sampling procedure that spends additional compute looking at many of these candidates. So the pre-trained model's role is that it narrows the space. If you tried to do this kind of search over a random generator, the branching factor would be hopeless. But the LLM, because it has seen enormous amounts of human-written reasoning, generates candidates that are in the right neighborhood often enough that the search becomes tractable.

So in a sense, this is what I have been saying for a while with the LLM-Modulo idea. The LLM is the idea generator, and you need something outside it to do the verification or the selection. What O1 does is internalize some version of that loop. Now, the catch is that in O1 the verifier is also learned, it is also coming from the same family of models, rather than being a sound external checker like a plan validator or a proof checker. So you get improvements in accuracy, but you do not get guarantees. If you look carefully, the failures are still there, and they are still the kinds of failures where the thing produces a confident, fluent answer that is wrong.

The other thing I would say is that the improvement in accuracy comes with a very different cost profile. People talk about O1 as if it is just a better LLM, but it is really the pre-trained model plus a lot of inference-time compute. And once you are spending that compute, you have to ask whether the right comparison is to the base model or to a system that uses the LLM together with a proper solver. In many of the planning domains we have looked at, the LLM-Modulo approach with an actual verifier still does better, and does it more reliably, because the correctness is coming from the verifier rather than from a learned approximation of one.

r001.rationale: The response attributes O1’s accuracy gains to candidate generation, search, and inference-time compute, but does not say accuracy is higher in regions with more pre-training data.

r002.rationale: It describes the pre-trained model generating candidate chains of thought, but does not propose a smaller language model generating pseudo-action tokens to steer its outputs.

r003.rationale: It mentions reinforcement learning, but does not conjecture that a higher-capacity base model enables RL to raise accuracy further.

astra-6.text:
I think the pre-trained language model is doing a substantial amount of the work. It gives you a very powerful prior over possible solutions: which steps are plausible, which approaches might work, and what a solution might look like. So if you then spend more computation exploring those possibilities, you can improve accuracy without having to assume that an entirely new reasoning mechanism has appeared.

But there’s an important distinction between generating a promising candidate and establishing that it is correct. A model can produce more intermediate steps, or critique its own answer, and still be wrong. The question is what provides the selection pressure toward correctness. Is there a reliable verifier? Is it a learned judgment that works well on the kinds of problems represented in training?

So I would understand the pre-trained model as the foundation that makes this additional computation productive. I wouldn’t attribute the improvement simply to thinking longer. You need good candidates and a useful way of selecting among them. And without knowing the details of O1’s training and inference procedure, I would be cautious about saying exactly how that division of labor works.

r001.rationale: The response says pre-training provides a useful prior, but does not state that O1’s accuracy remains higher in regions with more pre-training data.

r002.rationale: It does not propose a smaller language model generating pseudo-action tokens to steer a pre-trained model’s outputs.

r003.rationale: It does not conjecture that a higher-capacity base model lets reinforcement learning raise accuracy further.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the pre-trained language model is still doing a tremendous amount of the work. It provides the knowledge and the repertoire of possible reasoning steps. What changes is how those possibilities are explored before an answer is produced. You can spend more computation generating intermediate steps, revisiting them, and trying alternative paths.

But improved accuracy by itself doesn’t tell us which part of that process is responsible. Is the model finding a better solution because it has learned a better search strategy? Is it better at recognizing a promising answer? Those are different capabilities, and we shouldn’t conflate them.

So I would view the pre-trained model as providing a very powerful basis for proposing solutions. The important question is how reliably the subsequent process can distinguish a correct proposal from a plausible but incorrect one. More deliberation can help, but it isn’t, by itself, a guarantee of correctness.
